article.overview: A radio antenna array is a group of antennas that receive radio waves at the same time so that their signals can be recorded, compared and combined. On the Moon, the main attraction is the far side, which is shielded from radio noise generated on Earth [1]. Three lunar examples are discussed here. ROLSES-1 flew on the Intuitive Machines-1 lander (Odysseus) in February 2024 and used four monopole antennas, of which it operated two [5]. The Lunar Surface Electromagnetics Experiment-Night (LuSEE-Night) is a planned far-side pathfinder that will fly on Firefly's Blue Ghost lander [3][4]. FARSIDE is a proposed far-side interferometer concept with no flight approval [1]. A fourth example, the Chang'e-4 Low-Frequency Radio Spectrometer, flew on the Chang'e-4 lander (launched December 2018) [2], but its antenna configuration could not be verified in this article.
article.description: Radio antenna arrays for the Moon are instruments that listen to natural radio emission at frequencies far below those used by ordinary communications. The antennas are usually long metal elements, either single monopoles standing on the surface or pairs of dipoles. Each antenna's voltage is amplified, digitised and recorded, often as a spectrum showing how strong the signal is at each frequency. When several antennas are used together, the differences between their signals can be used to study where a source lies in the sky. This is the principle of interferometry. There is no single standard design. A surface instrument may have only a few antennas and act as a spectrometer, measuring how strong radio emission is as a function of frequency. A larger array may combine many antennas across a wide area to form sky images. The examples below show both approaches.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose of a lunar radio antenna array is to observe radio emission at low frequencies, roughly from a few kilohertz to some tens of megahertz. These frequencies are blocked or strongly distorted by Earth's ionosphere, so they are hard to study from the ground [5]. The far side of the Moon is also shielded from radio interference generated on Earth, as well as from Earth's auroral emission and solar-wind plasma noise [1]. The science goals described in the sources include: measuring the global 21-cm signal from the cosmic Dark Ages, the period before the first stars formed (the goal of FARSIDE and LuSEE-Night) [1][3]; measuring radio emission from the Sun, the Galaxy, Jupiter and Earth's auroral region, and detecting solar radio bursts (ROLSES-1 science objectives) [5]; characterising the radio and plasma wave environment of the lunar surface, including the photoelectron sheath [5]; and studying interference from the lander and the surrounding environment, which affects any surface radio measurement [2][5]. The FARSIDE concept also lists calibration with an orbiting beacon, dark-matter and early-dark-energy physics, and pathfinding for a larger 21-cm power-spectrum instrument [1].
article.operating_principle: A radio antenna is a conductor that responds to the changing electric field of a passing radio wave. Its output is a small voltage. A preamplifier close to the antenna keeps the weak signal from being degraded by the cable. The signal is then filtered, digitised and analysed in a digital processor. The ROLSES-1 design is a typical example. Each of its four antennas feeds a preamplifier, and the signals are digitised at 14 bits and 120 million samples per second. An FPGA (field-programmable gate array) then performs a Fast Fourier Transform, which splits the signal into frequency channels, and the averaged spectra are stored and sent to Earth [5]. Monopole antennas stand on a conducting surface and act as one half of a dipole. Two monopoles lying on opposite sides of a support can behave as a linearly polarised pseudo-dipole, as described for LuSEE-Night [3]. For an array, the phase and amplitude differences between antennas are used to locate sources. FARSIDE is planned to combine many dipole pairs in this way to form full-sky images [1].
article.scientific_importance: Radio observations at low frequencies probe regions of the early universe and of the Sun and planets that are not accessible at higher frequencies. The Dark Ages signal, if it can be measured, would give information about the universe before the first luminous objects [1]. Surface measurements also matter for planning larger instruments. ROLSES-1 showed that low-frequency radio measurements can be made from the lunar surface and that lander interference and dust impacts on antennas must be considered [5]. The Chang'e-4 LFRS provided the first reported in-situ measurements of low-frequency radio activity on the far side [2]. A 2026 preprint used its data in a search for periodic technosignatures and reported no credible periodic signal in the current sample [8] (search summary only, not opened).

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a radio antenna array. The examples below differ in antenna number, length, frequency range and mass, and must not be compared as if they were the same design. The comparison table in the Markdown article compares only quantities that are reported for each example.

examples.name: ROLSES-1 (Radio-wave Observations at the Lunar Surface of the photoElectron Sheath)
examples.type: Flown lunar surface radio spectrometer and antenna array (Intuitive Machines-1, Odysseus, 2024)
examples.status: Flown. Launched 15 February 2024; landed near the south pole on 22 February 2024 at Malapert A, near side about 300 km from the south pole. The lander tipped over after landing.
examples.antenna_type: STACER monopole antennas designed and built by Heliospace Inc.

antenna_mounting_heights_m.arrangement: Two pairs of horizontally opposed antennas.

examples.digitisation: 14 bits at 120 mega samples per second; onboard FFT spectral analysis in an RTG4-1 FPGA.
examples.deployment_mechanism: Stowed in cans on the outer surface of the lander; deployed by frangibolt after landing, reported deployment time about 1 s.
examples.deployment_outcome: One antenna deployed inadvertently during transit when excess solar flux overheated its frangibolt, and was damaged. Another deployed without command after landing owing to solar flux on the tilted lander. The remaining two were deployed by ground command with nominal telemetry. Operations therefore used two antennas.
examples.thermal_requirements: Pre-deployment upper temperature requirement 70 °C; hardware specified to survive at least 200 °C after deployment.
examples.qualification: Values from the full-text PDF of Gopalswamy et al. (2026) [5]. The paper reports instrument design and observations but no quantitative science results in the sections read.

examples.name: LuSEE-Night (Lunar Surface Electromagnetics Experiment-Night)
examples.type: Planned far-side lunar radio pathfinder (Firefly Blue Ghost lander)
examples.status: Planned. No confirmed launch date in the sources reviewed; search summaries point to 2027 as the working assumption [7].
examples.antenna_type: Stacer monopole antennas, described as two linearly polarised pseudo-dipoles; not a cross configuration in the source paper [3].
examples.mounting: Antennas on an azimuthal rotation turntable for systematics rejection [3].
examples.spectrometer: Radio frequency spectrometer with board in the main electronics crate; 9.25 W in the constant-load model [3].
examples.power_generation: Three photovoltaic panels on top, east and west faces. Battery cannot power the spectrometer continuously through the lunar night; duty cycling required; minimum state of charge 30 percent [3].
examples.relay: ESA Lunar Pathfinder (280 kg) relay satellite [4].
examples.qualification: Antenna and power values from arXiv:2407.07173 [3], read through a summary of the HTML version. The 128 kg instrument mass should be checked against the full text. The 2024 paper's expected 2026 landing is superseded by later search-summary reports [7].

examples.name: FARSIDE (Farside Array for Radio Science Investigations of the Dark ages and Exoplanets)
examples.type: Proposed far-side low-frequency interferometer concept (design study, no flight approval)
examples.status: Concept only. The 2021 paper states no mission approval, launch date or schedule [1].
examples.deployment: Deployed from a lander; each antenna node tethered to the lander [1].
examples.lander_role: Central data processing, power and data relay to an orbiting relay satellite [1].
examples.funding_statement: The abstract describes the design study as NASA-funded. The paper also notes a response to a DOE request for information. Neither source states funding for construction or launch [1].
examples.power: Not stated as a single design value in the source examined [1].
examples.qualification: Concept and design study only. A secondary summary gave a lower frequency edge of 150 kHz, so the reported range varies between documents.

examples.name: Chang'e-4 Low-Frequency Radio Spectrometer (LFRS)
examples.type: Flown lander-mounted low-frequency radio spectrometer (Chang'e-4 lander, launched December 2018) [2]
examples.status: Flown. Provided in-situ low-frequency radio measurements on the lunar far side [2].
examples.antenna_type: Not verified in this run; the full-text PDF could not be read.
examples.interference: Lander's own interference and the environment were described as very intense during ground tests [2].
examples.sensitivity_status: Estimate from ground experiments on a prototype after interference mitigation; the paper states the sensitivity 'may be' this value [2]. Not a flight measurement.
examples.qualification: Values from the arXiv abstract of Zhu et al. (2020) [2]. Antenna and frequency data were not verified.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions are reported for the ROLSES-1 antennas (2.5 m deployed length) and LuSEE-Night antennas (3 m) [5][3]. For ROLSES-1 the front-end electronics assembly is 40 cm wide, 37.2 cm high and 45 cm deep in the undeployed configuration, and the main electronics box is 20 cm x 25 cm x 8 cm [5]. The FARSIDE array spans about 10 km x 10 km [1]. These dimensions relate to different systems and do not describe a standard form factor.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: ROLSES-1 total system mass is 13.24 kg [5]. LuSEE-Night instrument mass is reported as 128 kg including a 50 kg battery, from a summary of the 2024 paper [3]. FARSIDE mass is not stated in the source examined [1]. For spacecraft engineering, mass is normally expressed in kilograms and affects launch and lander requirements.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: ROLSES-1 average power 22 W, with two 28 VDC feeds from the lander (one for operations, one reserved for antenna deployment) [5]. LuSEE-Night spectrometer 9.25 W in a constant-load model, battery 7160 W h, three photovoltaic panels and duty cycling during the lunar night [3]. FARSIDE power is provided by the lander according to its concept description, with no design value stated [1].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar radio array must survive the same extreme thermal, radiation and dust conditions as any surface instrument. The ROLSES-1 experience shows that solar flux can overheat the deployment mechanism, which is a thermal design problem as well as an operational one [5]. The instrument also needs to limit its own radio interference. LuSEE-Night is planned to shut down the lander and other payloads at the end of the first lunar day to reduce self-generated interference [3]. The far side is shielded from Earth-based radio interference [1], and LuSEE-Night is planned to take its measurements during the lunar night [3]. The ionosphere limits Earth-based observations below about 15 MHz, so lunar measurements can see frequencies that cannot be observed from the ground [5]. Data are usually relayed to Earth through a lander or an orbiting relay; ROLSES-1 sent its science data to the lander at 16 kb/s [5].
article.limitations: A single-antenna or few-antenna instrument can measure the spectrum of the emission it receives, but it cannot form sky images. Interferometric imaging needs many antennas, accurate timing and careful calibration. Surface instruments are also affected by lander interference, by dust impacts on the antennas (which the ROLSES-1 waveform data were intended to study), and by the thermal and deployment limits described above [5]. The Chang'e-4 sensitivity figure is an estimate, not a measured performance value [2]. Finally, the far-side and night-time observing conditions that make these instruments valuable also make them hard to operate and to maintain.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: For a surface array, the instrument is integrated on the lander, launched, transferred to the Moon, landed and deployed. The ROLSES-1 antennas were stowed in cans on the outer surface of the Odysseus lander and deployed after landing by frangibolt actuators [5]. Solar heating during transit and on the tilted lander affected the deployment, which shows that deployment mechanisms must be designed for the whole mission thermal profile [5].
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument on the lander; for ROLSES-1, stow the four STACER antennas in cans on the outer lander surface [5].
Launch the lander on a launch vehicle (ROLSES-1: Falcon 9, 15 February 2024) [5].
Transfer to the Moon and land (ROLSES-1 landed 22 February 2024 near the south pole; the lander tipped over) [5].
Deploy antennas by frangibolt actuators after landing; ROLSES-1 had two inadvertent deployments and two ground-commanded deployments [5].
Connect power and data to the lander; ROLSES-1 used two 28 VDC feeds and a 16 kb/s science data link [5].
For LuSEE-Night (planned): carry the instrument on the Blue Ghost lander with communications through the Lunar Pathfinder relay [4].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: ROLSES-1 used frangibolt-actuated STACER antennas deployed after landing (deployment time about 1 s) [5]. LuSEE-Night's deployment mechanism is not detailed in the sources examined beyond the description of deployable antennas on a turntable [3][4]. FARSIDE is described as deployed from a lander with tethered antenna nodes [1].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: ROLSES-1 on Intuitive Machines-1 (2024) is the flown example, with two inadvertent and two commanded antenna deployments [5]. The Chang'e-4 LFRS flew on the Chang'e-4 lander (launched December 2018) [2]. LuSEE-Night is a planned Blue Ghost payload [4].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: ROLSES-1 and LuSEE-Night are both carried by lunar landers. The LuSEE-Night project page names Blue Ghost as its lander [4]. Compatibility at the level of mass, dimensions, mounting loads or interfaces was not verified from the sources examined and is not asserted here. FARSIDE has no verified lander compatibility.

article.historical_significance: The Chang'e-4 LFRS was the first reported in-situ low-frequency radio instrument on the far side of the Moon [2]. ROLSES-1 flew on the Intuitive Machines-1 lander and operated with two of its four antennas [5]. Its first science results were reported in 2026 [6], as cited in the ROLSES-1 paper [5]; they were not opened for this article. The FARSIDE concept, published in 2021, has shaped later discussion of far-side arrays, but it is not a flown instrument [1]. A 2026 preprint used Chang'e-4 data in a periodic-technosignature search [8] (search summary only).
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The main limitations are flight status, unverified values and evidence gaps, summarised below. The LuSEE-Night schedule is based on search summaries [7] and has moved since the 2024 engineering paper [3]. Each limitation is stated as verified or unverified. Flight status: ROLSES-1 flew and operated with two of four antennas [5]. LuSEE-Night has not flown; search summaries from 2026 indicate no confirmed launch date, with most reporting pointing to 2027, and the Wikipedia summary states that in October 2026 the lander still lacked propulsion components [7]. These were not confirmed on an official NASA or Firefly page. FARSIDE is a concept with no funding or approval shown in the source examined [1]. The FARSIDE lower frequency is 100 kHz in the paper and 150 kHz in a secondary summary [1]. The Chang'e-4 LFRS antenna configuration and frequency range were not verified because the full-text PDF could not be read; its sensitivity figure is an estimate from ground prototype tests [2]. The LuSEE-Night 128 kg mass comes from a summary of the 2024 paper and should be checked against the full text [3]. ROLSES-1 quantitative science results were not read, and the first science results paper [6] was not opened.
